### I. The Threshold of the Wash

The mouth of the estuary does not believe in edges. Here, where the river Ouse unspools its final, copper-colored braids into the gray basin of the Wash, the world is renegotiated twice every twenty-four hours. It is an architecture made entirely of provisional surfaces: cockle-beds that gleam like hammered pewter under an overcast sky, banks of blue-gray silt that suck at the boots with a moist, pneumatic sigh, and long, low runs of samphire that turn the color of oxidized copper in the late autumn chill.

To live on this littoral is to understand that geography is not an absolute, but an agreement between gravity and liquidity, subject to cancellation without notice. 

My work here—if it can be dignified with the name of work—is that of an un-commissioned surveyor. For thirty-seven years, housed in the former customs house at the tip of the marsh, I have kept the *Ledgers of the Littoral*. The customs office was shuttered during the reign of the third George, when the channel shifted three miles to the east after a single night of gale-force northeasterlies, leaving the stone jetty stranded among the sheep pastures. The Crown simply forgot the building existed, or perhaps decided that a stone cottage slowly being engulfed by sea-lavender was not worth the trouble of an eviction. 

Inside, the salt has penetrated everything. It sits in the threads of my wool coats, crystalline and stiffening; it forms white, frosted ferns along the lower panes of the north-facing windows; it has migrated into the very paper of my blank folios, so that when the steel nib of my pen moves across the surface, it scratches with a dry, sand-like rasp, drinking ink not in clean strokes, but in slight, feathered haloes.

Every morning, depending on the tide tables pinned to the door with an iron carpet tack, I take up the mahogany plane table, the brass alidade, and the long ash surveyor’s rod with its blackened decimeter markings. I walk out across the sea wall—that great mound of turf and clay raised by seventeenth-century Dutchmen who thought they could teach the sea English manners—and descend into the zones of doubt.

People imagine that land meets water as a line: a stroke drawn with a fine-tipped pen upon an Admiralty chart. But down here, between the hard ground of the parish of Terrington and the deep water where the colliers run, there is a zone two leagues wide that is neither element. It is mud that acts like water, and water that has the consistency of cooling porridge. It is a territory where men drown not by sinking, but by being adhered to; they are simply held fast until the moon brings the North Sea back over their shoulders.

---

### II. The Taxonomy of Silt

The locals have nine words for the mud, though none of them are spoken with any affection. 

There is *slub*, which is the fresh, velvet deposit left by a retreating spring tide—soft, almost entirely liquid, smelling faintly of rotting wrack and cold iron. There is *gault*, which is the ancient, subterranean clay that underlies the marsh, blue-black and stiff as frozen butter, full of prehistoric oak roots that ring like bell-metal when struck by an iron spade. There is *warp*, which is the farmer’s friend, the fine river-borne silt that settles in the slack-water dykes and can be shoveled onto the potato fields to sweeten the sour fen peat. 

And then there is *the maw*. The maw is not a layer, but a condition. It occurs where a subterranean freshwater seep bubbles up through the tidal sediment, liquefying the silt from below while leaving a dry, crusted skin upon the surface. A gull can land upon it safely; a terrier will feel it tremble and turn back with its tail tucked; a man in rubber waders will take two steps, hear a sound like a wet leather glove smacking a tabletop, and find himself up to his hips before his brain has registered the absence of resistance.

In my journals, I do not use these dialect terms. I record the earth in degrees of resistance, measured by a brass-tipped rod dropped from a uniform height of four feet:

> *14 October. Wind WNW, force 3. Low water at 08:14. Station IV (The Spoil Bank). Penetration of the standard probe: 34.2 centimeters. Silt has grayed toward the hue of wet slate. Odor of hydrogen sulphide minimal; high proportion of pulverized shell-meal (Cardium edule). The western gully has migrated seven yards toward the beacon. The beacon itself leans four degrees further southward.*

Why measure what cannot be kept? 

My nephew, who visited me once from Norwich twelve years ago, wearing trousers that smelled of dry-cleaner’s naptha and carrying a small brass pocket watch he checked every twelve minutes, asked me this question as we sat over a meal of boiled herrings and tea.

"You are mapping water, Uncle," he said, not unkindly. He was an actuary for an insurance syndicate that insured herring drifters. "By the time your ink is dry, the channel you have drawn has filled with sand, and another has opened behind your back. It has no commercial value. The Admiralty has steam-launches with sounding-poles; they update the fairways once a year for the coasters. What you are doing is only poetry written with an architect's ruler."

I gave him the larger herring and did not answer him until the kettle had boiled again.

"The Admiralty," I said then, "is concerned only with where ships may float without scraping their keels. They care for the negative space—the void through which their tonnage moves. I am concerned with the flesh of the earth. I am cataloguing its decay. When an old man’s face wrinkles, it does no good to tell him that his skin is merely failing to remain flat for the purposes of navigation. He wants to know the history of the crevice beside his eye."

He nodded, but he slept with his watch under his pillow, and he left by the noon carrier the next day, shaking the salt from his boots upon the doorstep as if he could rid himself of the place by an act of will.

---

### III. The Drowned Parish

Three miles out from the sea-bank, at the place where the low-water spring tide retreats furthest, lies the church of Saint-Jude-in-the-Fens. 

It has not been a parish since the great inundation of November 1287, when the sea broke through the dunes from Hunstanton to Skegness, carrying away twelve villages and turning thirty thousand acres of barley into salt marsh. The stone of Saint-Jude’s was Barnack rag from the quarries near Stamford, dragged fifty miles down the Welland on barges. It was built to endure the judgment of God, and it has endured it, though not in the manner the masons intended.

At ordinary low tides, nothing is visible but a dark spine of stone, like the carcass of an overturned whale, around which the tide-races boil with a white, irritable foam. But on the great equinoctial springs—those vast, planetary sinkings of the sea that occur when the sun and moon pull in straight alignment—the water pulls back so far that the floor of the nave is laid bare to the sky.

I have visited it seven times in my life. Each visit requires a precise calculation of minutes. One has ninety minutes between the water falling below the sill and its return; to be caught there is to have your retreat cut off by two deep guts—the Cockle Channel and the Black Shore—forty minutes before the church itself is covered.

To walk down that nave is an experience that unstrings the mind. 

The flagstones are still there, slick with emerald green slime and carpeted with miniature colonies of blue mussels, each shell no larger than a grain of rice, packed together like the tiles of a Byzantine floor. The column bases remain, thick octagons of shelly limestone, their surfaces honeycombed by piddock clams whose white, brittle shells still rattle in the holes they bored seven centuries ago.

There are no monuments left, save one: a recumbent effigy of a knight whose name has been licked away by seven hundred years of North Sea silt. His face is gone—he has now only that smooth, featureless lump of chalk where a human nose and forehead were once carved, resembling nothing so much as a seal emerging from an ice hole. His hands, which were once raised in prayer, have been worn down into two rounded pebbles pressed against his breast. 

Standing there, with the wind bringing the smell of the Dogger Bank over forty miles of cold water, one understands what stone really is. It is not permanent; it is merely an extremely slow fluid. Under the tongue of the tide, Barnack limestone behaves exactly like sugar under a tap; it only requires more patience from the observer.

The last time I stood beside that knight, in September of the year before last, I noticed that the iron cramp holding his shoulder together—inserted, perhaps, during some forgotten repair in the reign of Edward II—had finally rusted through. The rust had stained the limestone a brilliant, violent orange, like a fresh arterial wound across the dead gray of the mud. I laid my hand upon his chest. The stone was colder than the water. It seemed to have stored within itself every winter that had passed over it since the fenmen had brought it from the inland quarry.

I took out my pocket-slate and drew his outline: not as he must have looked when they laid him down with candles burning at his corners, but as he was that afternoon—a calcium bone protruding from the earth’s wet lip. 

When I turned to look back toward the land, the sea wall had vanished. A low bank of sea-haze, what we call the *haar*, had drifted in from the Wash, erasing the coast. There was no north, no south; only the gray slate of the sky meeting the gray slate of the mudflats, and myself standing in the nave of a church whose roof was three fathoms of cold brine.

A man could have died of loneliness in three seconds. But I had my compass, its brass case heavy and reassuring in my palm, its needle trembling with that mysterious, unswerving fidelity to something invisible that lies thousands of miles to the north. I took my bearing—two hundred and twelve degrees, southwest-by-south—and walked, my feet making a rhythmic, sucking *clop* in the sludge, while behind me the first cold tongues of the flood tide began to lap against the knight’s smoothed chin.

---

### IV. The Mechanics of Optical Decay

The eye is not designed for the flats. 

Human vision evolved in woods and savannas, where edges are plentiful and distance is marked by the graduated overlapping of forms—this branch before that trunk, that hill before the blue mountain. On the Wash, there are no intermediaries. There is the foreground, which consists of the mud immediately around your boot-heels, and there is the horizon, which is twenty miles away and usually indistinct. Everything between is subject to atmospheric sorcery.

On warm afternoons in May, when the sun strikes the mudflats while the water is still chilled from the winter, the marsh produces the *fata morgana*. The warm air sits in layers over the cold silt like sheets of glass of varying thickness, bending the light rays until the world is unstitched at its seams.

I have seen a pair of black-tailed godwits, wading in four inches of water half a mile distant, appear as tall as church spires, their long legs shimmering like the pillars of an Italian portico. I have seen the red brick chimney of the drainage engine at Sutton Bridge—a modest tube thirty feet high—inverted and floating five hundred feet in the air, its smoke pouring downward into an imaginary sky.

Once, in my twenty-second year, I set out across the sandbars to retrieve what I was convinced was the wreck of an eighteenth-century schooner that had emerged from the shifting sands of the Roaring Middle. I saw its black ribs distinctly: the curvature of the oak knees, the stump of the bowsprit pointing accusingly at the Lincolnshire coast, even the remnants of rigging trailing in the brine. I walked for an hour toward it, the water never rising above my ankles. 

As I approached, the ship shrank. 

It lost its three decks; it lost its bowsprit; it shed its oak knees. When I finally reached it, it was an old sheep-trough of tarred deal, scarcely three feet long, jammed upright in a runnel by the tide and encrusted with five or six dry acorn barnacles. 

The mind makes what it can out of the meager data the marsh provides. It is hungry for significance; it cannot abide the fact that three square leagues of the world contain nothing whatsoever except salt, sand, and the indifferent screams of gulls.

This decay of the optical sense has its counterpart in the auditory. 

Sound travels over the flats with an unnatural, treacherous clarity. On a still night, when the mud is "sleeping"—that is, during the three days of the neap tides when the water moves with scarcely more force than a heavy sigh—I can hear the thump of an oar against a rowlock at the Boston Deeps, twelve miles across the bay. I can hear the whistle of the night train leaving King’s Lynn, nine miles inland, its sound bent downward by the cold ceiling of the mist until the engine seems to be rattling through my own vegetable patch.

Yet a man can scream for help fifty paces from you, down in the dead angle of a creek bank, and you will hear nothing but the wind blowing through the sedge. The mud swallows the voice; it is an acoustic sponge, porous and damp, that muffles human terror before it can travel three lengths of an ash pole.

---

### V. The Language of the Marsh

Language here does not accumulate words; it sheds them. 

The old people of the parishes around the marsh speak a dialect that has been ground down by the wind, like the pebbles on the beach at Heacham. It is an English that has discarded its polite auxiliaries, its decorative adjectives, its Latinate balances. It consists almost entirely of nouns that describe states of cold, damp, or rot, and verbs that relate to the movement of water and beasts.

An old drainer named Amos, who died in the winter the river froze from bank to bank, used to sit by my fire when his arthritis drove him from the ditches. He spoke of the earth as if it were a mule that had to be beaten into temporary compliance, though he knew it would eventually roll over and crush the man holding the whip.

"It won’t stay dug," he would tell me, staring into the peat smoke with eyes as pale and watery as the winter sky. "You can put three thousand men into the fens with spade and barrow, like the Dutchman Vermuyden did. You can cut your New Bedford rivers and your forty-foot drains. You can put up windmills and steam-pumps and scoop-wheels. But the fen *shrinks*. The minute you take the water out of the dirt, the dirt turns to dust and blows away down to the sea. The land goes down, down, down. Every year the fields are six inches lower than the drains that carry the water away. In the end, the river is running ten feet above your chimney-top, held in by dirt banks that are only held together by the roots of couch-grass. And the sea sits outside, waiting."

He was right. 

The paradox of the fens is that reclamation is merely an accelerated form of disappearance. When the great bogs were drained in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the ancient peat—composed of mosses and reeds preserved for three millennia under stagnant water—was exposed to the air. It oxidized; it caught fire from stray pipes and burned invisibly underground for months, turning into blue-white ash; it blew away in the great spring dust-storms that the farmers call the *fen-blows*, blackening the laundry on the lines forty miles away in Cambridge.

At the farm called Whittlesey Mere, they drove an iron post into the ground in 1848, through the peat down to the solid Oxford clay below, and cut the top level with the surface of the soil. Today, if you walk out into that field of sugar-beet, you must look up twelve feet to see the top of that post. The earth has literally vanished into thin air, leaving the measure of its own past suspended in the sky like a dried plum-line.

We are not building upon rock. We are building upon a crust of desiccated vegetable matter that is evaporating beneath our soles.

Amos knew this, though he had never read a book of geology in his life. 

"The sea wants it back," he said once, before he rose to walk his five miles home through the sleet. "And what the sea wants, the sea generally gets. It has more time than we have. It doesn't have to eat its dinner by six o'clock."

---

### VI. An Inventory of Found Things

My custom-house is not large, but it has eight rooms, six of which are empty of furniture. Over the years, these rooms have become a repository for the flotsam that the tide leaves behind—not the valuable wreckage that the coastguards look for (the casks of rum or the timber logs that bear the timber-merchant’s mark), but the smaller, incomprehensible leavings of human life that have been tumbled through the sand until their origins are lost.

In the south parlor, I keep what I call *The Cabinet of Inconsequence*.

There is a wooden shoe, carved from a single block of birch, of a pattern that has not been worn in England since the time of Charles the First. It was washed out of the peat beds at low water, preserved as perfectly as the day it was dropped into the bog, its wood turned the color of bitter chocolate, smelling of old vinegar.

There is a brass seal, three inches long, found in a gutter after the storm of 1897. It bears the arms of a merchant from Hamburg: three herrings and a pair of dividers, with the legend *SIGILLVM HEINRICI DE LVBEKE*. How did Heinrich of Lübeck lose his seal on the flats of Terrington? Did he lean over the gunwale of his cog in the fourteenth century to vomit into the Wash, and watch his credentials slip from his fingers into the black ooze? Or was he drowned here, his flesh eaten by the small brown crabs, his bones rolled along the sea-bed until this heavy little cylinder of brass was all that remained of his existence between the Elbe and the Welland?

There are seventy-four clay pipe bowls, their stems broken off short, their surfaces stained gray-brown by the marsh mud. Most of them bear the marks of makers from Lynn or Boston: *T.P.*, *W.C.*, *IOHN HUNT*. They are the cigarette ends of dead centuries, dropped by bargees as they waited for the tide to turn at the beacon, or by fowlers sitting in their flat-bottomed punts among the reed-ronds with their long matchlocks cocked for geese.

And there is one thing for which I have no classification: a ball of bees-wax, about the size of a goose’s egg, into which have been pressed hundreds of common iron pins. 

The pins have not rusted; the wax has preserved them from the salt. They are stuck in without any discernible order, so closely that their round heads form a continuous, metallic skin, like the scales of a carp. I found it four miles out, balanced upon a tuft of marsh-samphire, where the high spring tide had left it like an egg in a nest. 

Is it witchcraft? Some ancient fen-curse sent out to sea to drown its victim by sympathy? Or is it merely some cobbler’s contrivance, lost overboard from a wherry fifty years ago? 

I pick it up sometimes when the evening wind is high and the house groans in its lime-mortar joints. It is strangely heavy in the hand. The wax has absorbed the cold of the stones on which it lay; it never seems to warm to the palm. It represents an immense amount of labor—the patient sticking-in of pin after pin, four hundred or five hundred times, by some person whose hands are now dust, for a purpose that cannot now be reconstructed by any process of logic.

The world is full of these dead intentions. We imagine that our actions leave clear traces, like the track of an otter in the snow; but most human activity leaves only these blunt, unreadable tokens, scattered across the saltings until the sea rubs them down into pebbles.

---

### VII. The Migration of Names

Even the names of the places have lost their moorings.

On the oldest charts I possess—a set of hand-colored copperplate engravings executed by Captain Greenvile Collins in the 1680s—the channels bear names that are full of domestic confidence: *The Mother-Bank*, *The Three-Stone-Channel*, *The Maid’s Hole*, *The Friendly Passage*.

By the time the Ordnance Survey arrived in the 1880s with their steel chains and their six-inch scales, the *Mother-Bank* had become *The Knock*; *The Maid’s Hole* had been filled by a bank of shifting sand called *The Thief*; and *The Friendly Passage* was simply marked: *Unnavigable; dry at three hours’ ebb*.

The places themselves have not moved, if by "place" one means a specific set of numbers expressing latitude and longitude. But their character has migrated. 

A channel is not merely a depth of water; it is a habit of the sea. When the sea changes its habit, the name becomes a hollow skin, like the shell of a crab after the creature has crawled out to grow another.

I have spent the last seven months attempting to map the *Gore-Gull*.

In the town books of King's Lynn for the year 1542, it is recorded that the town paid twelve pence to a waterman for "placyng a marke-tree in the Gore-Gull to warne the botes from the sande." 

For three miles along the current bank, there is no gull—that is, no tidal creek—that could bear such a name. But if you walk the sheep-pastures a mile inland, through the land that was embanked under Queen Anne, you will find a long, curving depression in the turf, three yards wide and perhaps two feet deep, where the buttercups grow thicker and greener than they do elsewhere. 

That is the Gore-Gull. 

It is dead; it has been dry for two hundred and fifty years. The mark-tree has rotted; the waterman has been forgotten; the boats it warned are firewood or silt. But the ghost of the creek still runs through the meadow, and on nights when the rain falls with that steady, drenching fen-persistence that turns the grass into a lake, the water still collects in that slight depression and begins to run toward the sea, remembering its old path long after the men who cut it off have been buried in the churchyard at Clenchwarton.

This is what my ledgers are for. 

I do not record the land as it appears on a single day. I record the shadows of its former states, and the premonitions of its future ones. 

My maps are drawn on parchment that has been scraped three or four times, so that under the black ink of my current survey, you can still see the faint, brownish lines of the channel as it was in my father’s time, and the pale, yellow scratches that show where it ran when my grandfather was a boy.

A map that shows only what is currently dry is a lie. It is an instrument of commerce, not of truth. The truth is that the dry land is merely a temporary interruption of the sea, a brief hesitation in the universal tendency of all things to become mud.

---

### VIII. The Ledger of November

The light fails early now. 

It is half-past three in the afternoon, and the sun is already sinking behind the long line of the inland drainage bank, a flat, orange lozenge that does not warm the air. The mist is rising from the freshwater dykes, creeping across the pastures like white wool unrolling.

Out on the flats, the curlews are calling. 

It is the saddest sound in nature, that long, descending ripple of two notes, like a water-drop falling into a leaden vat. It has no melody; it is merely the cry of a creature that lives by thrusting its long, curved bill into cold slime to find worms that have never seen the sun. When there are five hundred of them together, as there are this evening on the Black Shore, their voices blend into a continuous, liquid murmur that sounds like the earth whispering to itself about its own dissolution.

I have come to the end of my fourteenth ledger. 

The book is three-quarters full of my tight, nineteenth-century clerk’s hand: columns of tides, tables of soundings, small sketches of sand-ribs and the silhouettes of navigational marks that were carried away by the February gales. 

My fingers are stiff with the cold. I keep an iron brazier beside the desk, filled with drift-coal that I gather from the beach—coal that was dropped from Newcastle colliers fifty years ago, black and hard as jet, that burns with a pale green flame and smells of the deep ocean. But the warmth does not extend two feet from the iron bars. My left hand, which rests on the ledger to hold the paper flat, is white at the knuckles and marbled with purple along the veins.

I am often asked—by myself, for there is no one else here to put the question—what will become of these thirty-six volumes when I have finished with them.

They are too detailed for the county library. They contain too many things that are of no practical use to any engineer or merchant. No one cares that on the eighth of August, 1904, the mud at the mouth of the Breast Sand was four inches softer than it had been on the same day in 1898; or that the skeleton of an ox, which had been buried near the beacon since the year of the cattle-plague, was exposed by the scouring of the channel, remained visible for three tides, and was then covered again by eighteen inches of fresh silt.

They will probably be thrown out when the customs service finally realizes that the cottage has an occupant who has ceased to draw a salary and whose name has fallen off their books. Some clerk with sleeve-protectors and an ink-stained ruler will come down from Lynn with a bailiff, look at the piles of folios stacked against the chimney-breast, sniff the smell of salt and dry-rot, and order them to be carter’s rubbish.

And that, perhaps, is as it should be.

It would be an insult to this coast to preserve its history in a library, where the air is dry and the books are protected from the rain. These pages belong to the silt they describe. They should be laid out upon the mudflats at low water, with stones on their corners to keep the wind from taking them, and left for the spring tide to read. 

The salt water would dissolve the gum-arabic in the ink; the iron-gall would turn from black to that pale, yellow-brown that you see on the sides of old ditches; the paper would soften, swell, and separate into its original linen rags; and in three tides, thirty-seven years of measurement would have returned to the general reservoir of mud, without leaving behind a single fraction of an inch of dry ground.

The moon is rising now, behind the church tower of Saint-Jude-in-the-Fen—not the drowned one, but its inland namesake that stands safely behind the sea wall at Walpole. 

It is a gibbous moon, pale as a bladder of lard, casting a cold, flat road of white across the three miles of wet slime that separate my window from the fairway. The water has turned; I can hear the first, low gurgle in the culvert beneath the floorboards—that sound like a horse drinking from a wooden trough that tells me the flood has entered the ditch.

I have one page left in this ledger. 

I shall not write down the soundings from the Spoil Bank. I shall not record the bearing of the beacon, which I know has moved another two inches to the east since yesterday’s gale. 

I will write only what the light is doing now, upon the skin of the water:

> *17 November. Night-tide. High water expected at 21:40. The moon has cleared the bank. The flats have ceased to be mud and have become light. For six miles there is no difference between the surface of the earth and the surface of the sky, both being of the color of milk in an iron pan. The channel is silent. The world is being covered up again, inch by inch, as it was in the beginning, and no one has been left outside.*

I shall close the book now, put the glass chimney back over the oil lamp, and bank the coal in the grate. The sea is coming up the steps of the jetty. It is four inches from the stone threshold; by ten o'clock it will be lapping at the third hinge of the coal-house door. 

It has done this every twelve hours since the world cooled. It will do it when the customs house has followed the drowned church into the sand, and when the ink in these ledgers has become nothing more than a faint gray smudge in a stratum of blue-black clay, waiting for some creature that does not yet exist to dig it up with a spade made of something that is not yet metal.

The Admiralty has steam-launches with sounding-poles; they update the fairways once a year for the coasters. What you are doing is only poetry written with an architect's ruler."

I gave him the larger herring and did not answer him until the kettle had boiled again.

"The Admiralty," I said then, "is concerned only with where ships may float without scraping their keels. They care for the negative space—the void through which their tonnage moves. I am concerned with the flesh of the earth. I am cataloguing its decay. When an old man’s face wrinkles, it does no good to tell him that his skin is merely failing to remain flat for the purposes of navigation. He wants to know the history of the crevice beside his eye."

He nodded, but he slept with his watch under his pillow, and he left by the noon carrier the next day, shaking the salt from his boots upon the doorstep as if he could rid himself of the place by an act of will.

---

### III. The Drowned Parish

Three miles out from the sea-bank, at the place where the low-water spring tide retreats furthest, lies the church of Saint-Jude-in-the-Fens. 

It has not been a parish since the great inundation of November 1287, when the sea broke through the dunes from Hunstanton to Skegness, carrying away twelve villages and turning thirty thousand acres of barley into salt marsh. The stone of Saint-Jude’s was Barnack rag from the quarries near Stamford, dragged fifty miles down the Welland on barges. It was built to endure the judgment of God, and it has endured it, though not in the manner the masons intended.

At ordinary low tides, nothing is visible but a dark spine of stone, like the carcass of an overturned whale, around which the tide-races boil with a white, irritable foam. But on the great equinoctial springs—those vast, planetary sinkings of the sea that occur when the sun and moon pull in straight alignment—the water pulls back so far that the floor of the nave is laid bare to the sky.

I have visited it seven times in my life. Each visit requires a precise calculation of minutes. One has ninety minutes between the water falling below the sill and its return; to be caught there is to have your retreat cut off by two deep guts—the Cockle Channel and the Black Shore—forty minutes before the church itself is covered.

To walk down that nave is an experience that unstrings the mind. 

The flagstones are still there, slick with emerald green slime and carpeted with miniature colonies of blue mussels, each shell no larger than a grain of rice, packed together like the tiles of a Byzantine floor. The column bases remain, thick octagons of shelly limestone, their surfaces honeycombed by piddock clams whose white, brittle shells still rattle in the holes they bored seven centuries ago.

There are no monuments left, save one: a recumbent effigy of a knight whose name has been licked away by seven hundred years of North Sea silt. His face is gone—he has now only that smooth, featureless lump of chalk where a human nose and forehead were once carved, resembling nothing so much as a seal emerging from an ice hole. His hands, which were once raised in prayer, have been worn down into two rounded pebbles pressed against his breast. 

Standing there, with the wind bringing the smell of the Dogger Bank over forty miles of cold water, one understands what stone really is. It is not permanent; it is merely an extremely slow fluid. Under the tongue of the tide, Barnack limestone behaves exactly like sugar under a tap; it only requires more patience from the observer.

The last time I stood beside that knight, in September of the year before last, I noticed that the iron cramp holding his shoulder together—inserted, perhaps, during some forgotten repair in the reign of Edward II—had finally rusted through. The rust had stained the limestone a brilliant, violent orange, like a fresh arterial wound across the dead gray of the mud. I laid my hand upon his chest. The stone was colder than the water. It seemed to have stored within itself every winter that had passed over it since the fenmen had brought it from the inland quarry.

I took out my pocket-slate and drew his outline: not as he must have looked when they laid him down with candles burning at his corners, but as he was that afternoon—a calcium bone protruding from the earth’s wet lip. 

When I turned to look back toward the land, the sea wall had vanished. A low bank of sea-haze, what we call the *haar*, had drifted in from the Wash, erasing the coast. There was no north, no south; only the gray slate of the sky meeting the gray slate of the mudflats, and myself standing in the nave of a church whose roof was three fathoms of cold brine.

A man could have died of loneliness in three seconds. But I had my compass, its brass case heavy and reassuring in my palm, its needle trembling with that mysterious, unswerving fidelity to something invisible that lies thousands of miles to the north. I took my bearing—two hundred and twelve degrees, southwest-by-south—and walked, my feet making a rhythmic, sucking *clop* in the sludge, while behind me the first cold tongues of the flood tide began to lap against the knight’s smoothed chin.

---

### IV. The Mechanics of Optical Decay

The eye is not designed for the flats. 

Human vision evolved in woods and savannas, where edges are plentiful and distance is marked by the graduated overlapping of forms—this branch before that trunk, that hill before the blue mountain. On the Wash, there are no intermediaries. There is the foreground, which consists of the mud immediately around your boot-heels, and there is the horizon, which is twenty miles away and usually indistinct. Everything between is subject to atmospheric sorcery.

On warm afternoons in May, when the sun strikes the mudflats while the water is still chilled from the winter, the marsh produces the *fata morgana*. The warm air sits in layers over the cold silt like sheets of glass of varying thickness, bending the light rays until the world is unstitched at its seams.

I have seen a pair of black-tailed godwits, wading in four inches of water half a mile distant, appear as tall as church spires, their long legs shimmering like the pillars of an Italian portico. I have seen the red brick chimney of the drainage engine at Sutton Bridge—a modest tube thirty feet high—inverted and floating five hundred feet in the air, its smoke pouring downward into an imaginary sky.

Once, in my twenty-second year, I set out across the sandbars to retrieve what I was convinced was the wreck of an eighteenth-century schooner that had emerged from the shifting sands of the Roaring Middle. I saw its black ribs distinctly: the curvature of the oak knees, the stump of the bowsprit pointing accusingly at the Lincolnshire coast, even the remnants of rigging trailing in the brine. I walked for an hour toward it, the water never rising above my ankles. 

As I approached, the ship shrank. 

It lost its three decks; it lost its bowsprit; it shed its oak knees. When I finally reached it, it was an old sheep-trough of tarred deal, scarcely three feet long, jammed upright in a runnel by the tide and encrusted with five or six dry acorn barnacles. 

The mind makes what it can out of the meager data the marsh provides. It is hungry for significance; it cannot abide the fact that three square leagues of the world contain nothing whatsoever except salt, sand, and the indifferent screams of gulls.

This decay of the optical sense has its counterpart in the auditory. 

Sound travels over the flats with an unnatural, treacherous clarity. On a still night, when the mud is "sleeping"—that is, during the three days of the neap tides when the water moves with scarcely more force than a heavy sigh—I can hear the thump of an oar against a rowlock at the Boston Deeps, twelve miles across the bay. I can hear the whistle of the night train leaving King’s Lynn, nine miles inland, its sound bent downward by the cold ceiling of the mist until the engine seems to be rattling through my own vegetable patch.

Yet a man can scream for help fifty paces from you, down in the dead angle of a creek bank, and you will hear nothing but the wind blowing through the sedge. The mud swallows the voice; it is an acoustic sponge, porous and damp, that muffles human terror before it can travel three lengths of an ash pole.

---

### V. The Language of the Marsh

Language here does not accumulate words; it sheds them. 

The old people of the parishes around the marsh speak a dialect that has been ground down by the wind, like the pebbles on the beach at Heacham. It is an English that has discarded its polite auxiliaries, its decorative adjectives, its Latinate balances. It consists almost entirely of nouns that describe states of cold, damp, or rot, and verbs that relate to the movement of water and beasts.

An old drainer named Amos, who died in the winter the river froze from bank to bank, used to sit by my fire when his arthritis drove him from the ditches. He spoke of the earth as if it were a mule that had to be beaten into temporary compliance, though he knew it would eventually roll over and crush the man holding the whip.

"It won’t stay dug," he would tell me, staring into the peat smoke with eyes as pale and watery as the winter sky. "You can put three thousand men into the fens with spade and barrow, like the Dutchman Vermuyden did. You can cut your New Bedford rivers and your forty-foot drains. You can put up windmills and steam-pumps and scoop-wheels. But the fen *shrinks*. The minute you take the water out of the dirt, the dirt turns to dust and blows away down to the sea. The land goes down, down, down. Every year the fields are six inches lower than the drains that carry the water away. In the end, the river is running ten feet above your chimney-top, held in by dirt banks that are only held together by the roots of couch-grass. And the sea sits outside, waiting."

He was right. 

The paradox of the fens is that reclamation is merely an accelerated form of disappearance. When the great bogs were drained in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the ancient peat—composed of mosses and reeds preserved for three millennia under stagnant water—was exposed to the air. It oxidized; it caught fire from stray pipes and burned invisibly underground for months, turning into blue-white ash; it blew away in the great spring dust-storms that the farmers call the *fen-blows*, blackening the laundry on the lines forty miles away in Cambridge.

At the farm called Whittlesey Mere, they drove an iron post into the ground in 1848, through the peat down to the solid Oxford clay below, and cut the top level with the surface of the soil. Today, if you walk out into that field of sugar-beet, you must look up twelve feet to see the top of that post. The earth has literally vanished into thin air, leaving the measure of its own past suspended in the sky like a dried plum-line.

We are not building upon rock. We are building upon a crust of desiccated vegetable matter that is evaporating beneath our soles.

Amos knew this, though he had never read a book of geology in his life. 

"The sea wants it back," he said once, before he rose to walk his five miles home through the sleet. "And what the sea wants, the sea generally gets. It has more time than we have. It doesn't have to eat its dinner by six o'clock."

---

### VI. An Inventory of Found Things

My custom-house is not large, but it has eight rooms, six of which are empty of furniture. Over the years, these rooms have become a repository for the flotsam that the tide leaves behind—not the valuable wreckage that the coastguards look for (the casks of rum or the timber logs that bear the timber-merchant’s mark), but the smaller, incomprehensible leavings of human life that have been tumbled through the sand until their origins are lost.

In the south parlor, I keep what I call *The Cabinet of Inconsequence*.

There is a wooden shoe, carved from a single block of birch, of a pattern that has not been worn in England since the time of Charles the First. It was washed out of the peat beds at low water, preserved as perfectly as the day it was dropped into the bog, its wood turned the color of bitter chocolate, smelling of old vinegar.

There is a brass seal, three inches long, found in a gutter after the storm of 1897. It bears the arms of a merchant from Hamburg: three herrings and a pair of dividers, with the legend *SIGILLVM HEINRICI DE LVBEKE*. How did Heinrich of Lübeck lose his seal on the flats of Terrington? Did he lean over the gunwale of his cog in the fourteenth century to vomit into the Wash, and watch his credentials slip from his fingers into the black ooze? Or was he drowned here, his flesh eaten by the small brown crabs, his bones rolled along the sea-bed until this heavy little cylinder of brass was all that remained of his existence between the Elbe and the Welland?

There are seventy-four clay pipe bowls, their stems broken off short, their surfaces stained gray-brown by the marsh mud. Most of them bear the marks of makers from Lynn or Boston: *T.P.*, *W.C.*, *IOHN HUNT*. They are the cigarette ends of dead centuries, dropped by bargees as they waited for the tide to turn at the beacon, or by fowlers sitting in their flat-bottomed punts among the reed-ronds with their long matchlocks cocked for geese.

And there is one thing for which I have no classification: a ball of bees-wax, about the size of a goose’s egg, into which have been pressed hundreds of common iron pins. 

The pins have not rusted; the wax has preserved them from the salt. They are stuck in without any discernible order, so closely that their round heads form a continuous, metallic skin, like the scales of a carp. I found it four miles out, balanced upon a tuft of marsh-samphire, where the high spring tide had left it like an egg in a nest. 

Is it witchcraft? Some ancient fen-curse sent out to sea to drown its victim by sympathy? Or is it merely some cobbler’s contrivance, lost overboard from a wherry fifty years ago? 

I pick it up sometimes when the evening wind is high and the house groans in its lime-mortar joints. It is strangely heavy in the hand. The wax has absorbed the cold of the stones on which it lay; it never seems to warm to the palm. It represents an immense amount of labor—the patient sticking-in of pin after pin, four hundred or five hundred times, by some person whose hands are now dust, for a purpose that cannot now be reconstructed by any process of logic.

The world is full of these dead intentions. We imagine that our actions leave clear traces, like the track of an otter in the snow; but most human activity leaves only these blunt, unreadable tokens, scattered across the saltings until the sea rubs them down into pebbles.

---

### VII. The Migration of Names

Even the names of the places have lost their moorings.

On the oldest charts I possess—a set of hand-colored copperplate engravings executed by Captain Greenvile Collins in the 1680s—the channels bear names that are full of domestic confidence: *The Mother-Bank*, *The Three-Stone-Channel*, *The Maid’s Hole*, *The Friendly Passage*.

By the time the Ordnance Survey arrived in the 1880s with their steel chains and their six-inch scales, the *Mother-Bank* had become *The Knock*; *The Maid’s Hole* had been filled by a bank of shifting sand called *The Thief*; and *The Friendly Passage* was simply marked: *Unnavigable; dry at three hours’ ebb*.

The places themselves have not moved, if by "place" one means a specific set of numbers expressing latitude and longitude. But their character has migrated. 

A channel is not merely a depth of water; it is a habit of the sea. When the sea changes its habit, the name becomes a hollow skin, like the shell of a crab after the creature has crawled out to grow another.

I have spent the last seven months attempting to map the *Gore-Gull*.

In the town books of King's Lynn for the year 1542, it is recorded that the town paid twelve pence to a waterman for "placyng a marke-tree in the Gore-Gull to warne the botes from the sande." 

For three miles along the current bank, there is no gull—that is, no tidal creek—that could bear such a name. But if you walk the sheep-pastures a mile inland, through the land that was embanked under Queen Anne, you will find a long, curving depression in the turf, three yards wide and perhaps two feet deep, where the buttercups grow thicker and greener than they do elsewhere. 

That is the Gore-Gull. 

It is dead; it has been dry for two hundred and fifty years. The mark-tree has rotted; the waterman has been forgotten; the boats it warned are firewood or silt. But the ghost of the creek still runs through the meadow, and on nights when the rain falls with that steady, drenching fen-persistence that turns the grass into a lake, the water still collects in that slight depression and begins to run toward the sea, remembering its old path long after the men who cut it off have been buried in the churchyard at Clenchwarton.

This is what my ledgers are for. 

I do not record the land as it appears on a single day. I record the shadows of its former states, and the premonitions of its future ones. 

My maps are drawn on parchment that has been scraped three or four times, so that under the black ink of my current survey, you can still see the faint, brownish lines of the channel as it was in my father’s time, and the pale, yellow scratches that show where it ran when my grandfather was a boy.

A map that shows only what is currently dry is a lie. It is an instrument of commerce, not of truth. The truth is that the dry land is merely a temporary interruption of the sea, a brief hesitation in the universal tendency of all things to become mud.

---

### VIII. The Ledger of November

The light fails early now. 

It is half-past three in the afternoon, and the sun is already sinking behind the long line of the inland drainage bank, a flat, orange lozenge that does not warm the air. The mist is rising from the freshwater dykes, creeping across the pastures like white wool unrolling.

Out on the flats, the curlews are calling. 

It is the saddest sound in nature, that long, descending ripple of two notes, like a water-drop falling into a leaden vat. It has no melody; it is merely the cry of a creature that lives by thrusting its long, curved bill into cold slime to find worms that have never seen the sun. When there are five hundred of them together, as there are this evening on the Black Shore, their voices blend into a continuous, liquid murmur that sounds like the earth whispering to itself about its own dissolution.

I have come to the end of my fourteenth ledger. 

The book is three-quarters full of my tight, nineteenth-century clerk’s hand: columns of tides, tables of soundings, small sketches of sand-ribs and the silhouettes of navigational marks that were carried away by the February gales. 

My fingers are stiff with the cold. I keep an iron brazier beside the desk, filled with drift-coal that I gather from the beach—coal that was dropped from Newcastle colliers fifty years ago, black and hard as jet, that burns with a pale green flame and smells of the deep ocean. But the warmth does not extend two feet from the iron bars. My left hand, which rests on the ledger to hold the paper flat, is white at the knuckles and marbled with purple along the veins.

I am often asked—by myself, for there is no one else here to put the question—what will become of these thirty-six volumes when I have finished with them.

They are too detailed for the county library. They contain too many things that are of no practical use to any engineer or merchant. No one cares that on the eighth of August, 1904, the mud at the mouth of the Breast Sand was four inches softer than it had been on the same day in 1898; or that the skeleton of an ox, which had been buried near the beacon since the year of the cattle-plague, was exposed by the scouring of the channel, remained visible for three tides, and was then covered again by eighteen inches of fresh silt.

They will probably be thrown out when the customs service finally realizes that the cottage has an occupant who has ceased to draw a salary and whose name has fallen off their books. Some clerk with sleeve-protectors and an ink-stained ruler will come down from Lynn with a bailiff, look at the piles of folios stacked against the chimney-breast, sniff the smell of salt and dry-rot, and order them to be carter’s rubbish.

And that, perhaps, is as it should be.

It would be an insult to this coast to preserve its history in a library, where the air is dry and the books are protected from the rain. These pages belong to the silt they describe. They should be laid out upon the mudflats at low water, with stones on their corners to keep the wind from taking them, and left for the spring tide to read. 

The salt water would dissolve the gum-arabic in the ink; the iron-gall would turn from black to that pale, yellow-brown that you see on the sides of old ditches; the paper would soften, swell, and separate into its original linen rags; and in three tides, thirty-seven years of measurement would have returned to the general reservoir of mud, without leaving behind a single fraction of an inch of dry ground.

The moon is rising now, behind the church tower of Saint-Jude-in-the-Fen—not the drowned one, but its inland namesake that stands safely behind the sea wall at Walpole. 

It is a gibbous moon, pale as a bladder of lard, casting a cold, flat road of white across the three miles of wet slime that separate my window from the fairway. The water has turned; I can hear the first, low gurgle in the culvert beneath the floorboards—that sound like a horse drinking from a wooden trough that tells me the flood has entered the ditch.

I have one page left in this ledger. 

I shall not write down the soundings from the Spoil Bank. I shall not record the bearing of the beacon, which I know has moved another two inches to the east since yesterday’s gale. 

I will write only what the light is doing now, upon the skin of the water:

> *17 November. Night-tide. High water expected at 21:40. The moon has cleared the bank. The flats have ceased to be mud and have become light. For six miles there is no difference between the surface of the earth and the surface of the sky, both being of the color of milk in an iron pan. The channel is silent. The world is being covered up again, inch by inch, as it was in the beginning, and no one has been left outside.*

I shall close the book now, put the glass chimney back over the oil lamp, and bank the coal in the grate. The sea is coming up the steps of the jetty. It is four inches from the stone threshold; by ten o'clock it will be lapping at the third hinge of the coal-house door. 

It has done this every twelve hours since the world cooled. It will do it when the customs house has followed the drowned church into the sand, and when the ink in these ledgers has become nothing more than a faint gray smudge in a stratum of blue-black clay, waiting for some creature that does not yet exist to dig it up with a spade made of something that is not yet metal.
